factStatement: An array holds items in order at numbered positions starting from zero.
familyName: Reading a value at a position
measurementObjective: Given an array, name the value at a stated position or the position of a value.
distractorStrategy: One-based counting; the last position given as the length; a negative position assumed invalid where the language allows it. Show the array with its values in the stem.

factStatement: The length is the number of items; the last position is one less than that.
familyName: Distinguishing length from last position
measurementObjective: Given an array, give its length and its last valid position.
distractorStrategy: The two treated as the same number; length counted from zero; an empty array assumed to have length one. Every off-by-one bug later traces to this.

conceptName: What you can do to an array
factStatement: Reading, replacing, inserting, removing and searching are distinct operations with different effects.
familyName: Recognising what an operation does
measurementObjective: Given a described change, name the operation and say whether the length changes.
distractorStrategy: Replacing confused with inserting — the length is the discriminator; removing assumed to leave a gap; searching assumed to change the array.

conceptName: What you can do to an array
factStatement: Inserting or removing in the middle moves every item after that position.
familyName: What happens to positions after an insertion
measurementObjective: Give the array contents and the new position of a named item after an insertion or removal.
distractorStrategy: Items assumed to stay at their old positions; the shift applied in the wrong direction; the item at the insertion point assumed overwritten. The overwriting case is the insert/replace confusion again, now traced.

factStatement: A traversal visits each item once, and what it does at each item decides the result.
familyName: What a traversal produces
measurementObjective: Give the result of a described traversal — a total, a count, a maximum — over stated data.
distractorStrategy: The total where a count was asked; a maximum computed from a wrong starting value; the first or last item missed. Show the data so the answer is checkable.

factStatement: Finding an item in unsorted data means checking items one by one, and the worst case checks all of them.
familyName: How much work an unsorted search does
measurementObjective: Give the number of comparisons a search makes for a stated target and data.
distractorStrategy: The best case given where the worst was asked; the count when the item is absent given as the length minus one; the position given instead of the comparison count. Ask about an absent item at D4.

factStatement: In sorted data a comparison can rule out half the remaining items, so far fewer checks are needed.
familyName: Reasoning about halving a sorted range
measurementObjective: Say which items remain in consideration after a stated comparison, or how many checks are needed.
distractorStrategy: Half discarded from the wrong side; the halving applied to unsorted data — the essential precondition; the count given as half the length rather than as repeated halving.
notes: The precondition matters more than the arithmetic and should be tested directly at D4.

factStatement: A simple sort makes repeated passes, and after each pass more of the data is in its final place.
familyName: The state of the data after one pass
measurementObjective: Given data and a described sorting method, give the arrangement after one or two passes.
distractorStrategy: The fully sorted result given where one pass was asked; a pass applied in the wrong direction; the largest item placed at the wrong end. The fully-sorted distractor catches students who know the outcome and not the process.
notes: Method described in words in the stem; no algorithm names required.

conceptName: How much work an operation costs
factStatement: Some operations take the same work whatever the size, and others take more as the data grows.
familyName: Comparing how two operations scale
measurementObjective: Given two operations, say which does more work as the data grows and why.
distractorStrategy: Reading a position assumed to cost more for a longer array; inserting at the end confused with inserting at the front; both assumed equal because both are one line of code. The last is the real misconception.
notes: In words and counts, never notation.

factStatement: Accessing a position that does not exist either fails or gives meaningless data, depending on the language.
familyName: Reasoning about an access past the end
measurementObjective: Say what happens when a traversal reads one position too far.
distractorStrategy: The access assumed always to fail loudly; assumed to return an empty value; assumed to wrap to the start. Loop bounds written with the length rather than length-minus-one is the natural stem.
notes: Complements CC_FAM09 from the algorithm side rather than the language side.

factStatement: Some problems are solved by moving two positions toward each other rather than by traversing twice.
familyName: Tracing two positions moving through data
measurementObjective: Given data and a described two-position method, say what the positions hold after several steps.
distractorStrategy: One position moved and not the other; the crossing condition applied one step late; the values swapped where only the positions moved. Reversing in place is the clearest stem.

factStatement: Whether the data is sorted, and how large it is, decides which approach is appropriate.
familyName: Choosing a search or traversal approach
measurementObjective: Given a stated requirement and the shape of the data, choose the appropriate approach.
distractorStrategy: A halving search on unsorted data; sorting first where one lookup is needed; a single traversal where every pair must be compared. The stated shape of the data must decide it.

factStatement: A result that is one item short, or misses the first or last item, points to a specific bound or starting-value fault.
familyName: Diagnosing an off-by-one from the result
measurementObjective: Given a traversal and a result that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A fault that would miss the other end; a fault that would give a different kind of wrongness; the data blamed rather than the bounds. The specific way it is wrong must implicate one fault.
notes: A maximum initialised to zero over all-negative data is the strongest D5 stem.

factStatement: Empty and single-item data break approaches that assume at least two items.
familyName: Behaviour on empty or single-item data
measurementObjective: Say what a described approach produces for empty or single-item data.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary-data answer; a failure where a wrong value is returned quietly; a value where it genuinely fails. Comparing adjacent pairs on a single item is the canonical case.

conceptName: How much work an operation costs
factStatement: Making one operation cheaper usually makes another dearer, so the right structure depends on what will be done most.
familyName: Judging a trade-off between operations
measurementObjective: Given the operations a program performs most, choose the arrangement of data that suits it.
distractorStrategy: Keeping data sorted where insertions dominate; leaving it unsorted where lookups dominate; a choice that ignores the stated usage. The usage pattern must decide, and both options must be workable.

factStatement: Text is a sequence of characters at numbered positions, including spaces and punctuation.
familyName: Reading a character at a position
measurementObjective: Given text, name the character at a position or the position of a character.
distractorStrategy: Spaces not counted as characters — the essential case; one-based positions; punctuation skipped. Text with a space in the middle must appear.

factStatement: The length counts every character, including spaces.
familyName: Counting the length of text
measurementObjective: Give the length of stated text.
distractorStrategy: Spaces omitted; words counted instead of characters; a trailing space missed. Use text where the difference is one or two, so careless counting shows.

factStatement: Two pieces of text differing only in case are not equal unless case is deliberately ignored.
familyName: Deciding whether two pieces of text match
measurementObjective: Say whether two pieces of text compare equal.
distractorStrategy: Case assumed ignored; a leading space assumed ignored; the comparison assumed to fail on length alone. Options must preserve case exactly — the case IS the content.
notes: Nothing downstream may compare these options case-insensitively.

factStatement: Taking a range of characters uses a start and an end, and whether the end is included is a fixed rule.
familyName: Working out what a range produces
measurementObjective: Give the text a stated range produces.
distractorStrategy: The end included when it is not; one character short at the start; the range read backwards. Off-by-one at each end is the whole family.

factStatement: Operations on text produce a new value and leave the original unchanged.
familyName: What the original holds after an operation
measurementObjective: Say what the original variable holds after an operation on it.
distractorStrategy: The original assumed modified in place — the central misconception; the result assumed discarded; both assumed to change. Requires an operation whose result is not assigned back.

factStatement: Searching text gives the position of the first match, or an indication that there is none.
familyName: What a search within text returns
measurementObjective: Give the result of searching for stated text, including when it is absent.
distractorStrategy: The last match returned rather than the first; a not-found result treated as position zero — the bug that makes absent text look present; the count of matches returned.
notes: The not-found-as-zero confusion is worth several items.

factStatement: Splitting text produces pieces determined by where the separator occurs, including empty pieces.
familyName: How many pieces splitting produces
measurementObjective: Given text and a separator, say how many pieces result and what they are.
distractorStrategy: Empty pieces from consecutive separators omitted; a leading or trailing separator ignored; the separator included in the pieces. Consecutive separators are the D4 case.

factStatement: Joining pieces places the separator between them, so there is one fewer separator than pieces.
familyName: What joining produces
measurementObjective: Give the text produced by joining stated pieces.
distractorStrategy: A separator added at the end; one fewer separator than needed; the pieces concatenated with no separator. The counting relationship is the measurement.

factStatement: Leading and trailing spaces are part of the text and change comparisons and lengths.
familyName: Reasoning about invisible characters
measurementObjective: Say why two pieces of text that look identical do not match.
distractorStrategy: The mismatch attributed to case where the cause is a space; to length where both are the same length; assumed impossible because they look the same. The stem must make the space visible in the description.
notes: The single most common cause of "but they are the same" in real input handling.

factStatement: Traversing text one character at a time can count occurrences or build new text.
familyName: What a character-by-character traversal produces
measurementObjective: Give the count or the text a described traversal produces.
distractorStrategy: Spaces included where they should be skipped and the reverse; the count off by one at an end; the built text in the wrong order. Counting vowels in text with a space is a good stem.

factStatement: Whether text reads the same backwards is decided by comparing characters from both ends.
familyName: Reasoning about a symmetry check
measurementObjective: Say whether stated text passes a described symmetry check, and how many comparisons it takes.
distractorStrategy: A check that ignores case where the stem says it should not; one that includes spaces where it should not; the comparison count given as the full length rather than half. Case and spaces must be specified in the stem.

conceptName: How much work text operations cost
factStatement: Building text by repeatedly adding to it does more work than assembling the pieces once.
familyName: Comparing the cost of two ways of building text
measurementObjective: Given two ways of building the same text, say which does more work and why.
distractorStrategy: The two assumed equivalent because the result is the same; the cost attributed to the number of lines of code; the cheaper method identified with the wrong reason. The reason must be that each addition copies.
notes: Depends on DS_FAM05: it costs more precisely because the original is never modified.

factStatement: Output missing its first or last character, or with a stray separator, points to a specific range or loop fault.
familyName: Diagnosing a text fault from the output
measurementObjective: Given text output that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A fault that would break the other end; a fault producing a different kind of wrongness; the input blamed. A trailing separator and a missing last character must be distinguishable from the output alone.

factStatement: Empty text and single-character text break approaches that assume at least two characters.
familyName: Behaviour on empty or single-character text
measurementObjective: Say what a described approach produces for empty or single-character text.
distractorStrategy: The ordinary answer; a failure where an empty result is returned quietly; a result where it genuinely fails. A symmetry check on empty text, which is trivially symmetric, is the sharpest case.

factStatement: Splitting, traversing and searching each suit different text tasks.
familyName: Choosing how to process text
measurementObjective: Given a text task, choose the approach that handles it, including its awkward inputs.
distractorStrategy: An approach that works on tidy input and fails on repeated separators; one that needs several passes where one suffices; one that solves a slightly different task. The awkward input must be stated.

factStatement: A table holds rows of the same shape, where each column holds one kind of value.
familyName: Identifying rows, columns and values
measurementObjective: Given a table in the stem, name a row, a column or a value.
distractorStrategy: A row named as a column; the header counted as a row; a column described as holding mixed kinds of value.

factStatement: A key is a column whose value identifies exactly one row and is never repeated.
familyName: Recognising which column could be a key
measurementObjective: Given a table, identify which column can serve as a key.
distractorStrategy: A column that happens to be unique in the sample but is not unique in principle — a name, a date of birth; a column with a repeat visible in the data; a column with a missing value. The name column is the essential distractor.
notes: The sample data must contain the counterexample.

factStatement: Each column holds one type of value, which decides how it can be compared and sorted.
familyName: Recognising the type a column should hold
measurementObjective: Given a column of sample values, say what type it should be.
distractorStrategy: A phone number typed as a number, which loses leading zeros — the productive case; a date stored as text; a yes/no stored as free text.

factStatement: The same fact stored in several rows can be updated in one and not the others, leaving the data contradicting itself.
familyName: Reasoning about what duplication causes
measurementObjective: Given a table with repeated data, say what goes wrong when one copy is changed.
distractorStrategy: Duplication described as merely wasteful — true but not the point; described as harmless because the values match today; the problem attributed to size rather than to consistency.
notes: The reason tables get split, and therefore the reason relationships exist.

factStatement: A column holding another table's key links a row to a row in that table.
familyName: Following a link between two tables
measurementObjective: Given two tables, say which row in one a stated row in the other refers to.
distractorStrategy: The link followed in the wrong direction; matched on a name column rather than the key; a row with no matching reference assumed to match the first. Show both tables.

factStatement: A relationship may allow one match or many, and which it is decides where the reference is stored.
familyName: Deciding whether a relationship is one-to-many
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, say how many rows on each side may correspond.
distractorStrategy: A one-to-many relationship read the wrong way round; a many-to-many treated as one-to-many; the reference placed on the side that would need repeating. The direction is the measurement.

factStatement: Moving a repeated fact into its own table leaves each fact recorded once.
familyName: Deciding what to move into its own table
measurementObjective: Given a table with repeated data, choose the split that records each fact once.
distractorStrategy: A split on a column that is not actually repeated; one that leaves the duplication in place; one that splits so far that a simple question needs three tables. Cost of over-splitting is the D4 case.
notes: Normalisation reasoning without the vocabulary or the numbered forms.

factStatement: A missing value is not the same as zero or as empty text, and comparisons against it do not behave normally.
familyName: Reasoning about a missing value
measurementObjective: Say how a missing value behaves in a comparison or a total.
distractorStrategy: Missing treated as zero in a total; treated as equal to another missing value; treated as matching an "is not" condition. All three are wrong for the same underlying reason.
notes: Foundation-critical: it silently changes counts and averages.

factStatement: A constraint refuses data that would break a rule, at the moment it is written.
familyName: Reasoning about what a constraint prevents
measurementObjective: Given constraints and an attempted insertion, say whether it is accepted.
distractorStrategy: A duplicate key accepted; a reference to a non-existent row accepted; a missing value accepted where the column requires one. Each must be decidable from the stated constraints.

factStatement: Rows are not stored in a guaranteed order; any order you rely on must be asked for.
familyName: Reasoning about the order rows come back in
measurementObjective: Say whether a described result is guaranteed to be in a particular order.
distractorStrategy: Insertion order assumed guaranteed; key order assumed guaranteed; the order seen once assumed stable. This is why "the first row" is not a well-defined idea.

factStatement: Answering a question that spans tables means matching rows on the linking column.
familyName: Working out the rows a combination produces
measurementObjective: Given two small tables, say how many rows the described combination yields.
distractorStrategy: The sum of the two row counts; the product, which is what happens with no matching condition; unmatched rows counted as though matched. The unmatched-row case is the important one.
notes: Prepares SQ_FAM11 without requiring SQL syntax.

factStatement: A count or total that is wrong usually comes from duplication, missing values, or an unmatched link.
familyName: Diagnosing a wrong count or total
measurementObjective: Given data and a wrong result, identify which of the three causes explains it.
distractorStrategy: Duplication blamed where a missing value is the cause; a missing value blamed where a row failed to match; the calculation blamed rather than the data. The data must distinguish them.

factStatement: A design choice made now decides which questions are easy and which become impossible to answer accurately.
familyName: Judging a design by the questions it permits
measurementObjective: Given a design and a question to be answered later, say whether the design can answer it.
distractorStrategy: A design that stores a computed total and so cannot answer about its parts; one that stores several values in one column; one that is fine. Storing "history" only as a current value is the strongest D5 case.
notes: The most transferable idea in the skill: a design forecloses questions.

factStatement: Empty tables and rows with no match are where a query or a report gives a misleading answer.
familyName: Reasoning about empty or unmatched data
measurementObjective: Say what a described report shows when a table is empty or rows do not match.
distractorStrategy: An error assumed where a zero or an empty result is returned; a total of zero presented as reliable; unmatched rows assumed included. Averaging over an empty result is the canonical case.

factStatement: Choosing a real-world value as a key ties the data to something that can change.
familyName: Judging a choice of key
measurementObjective: Given candidate keys, choose the one that stays valid and say what breaks with the others.
distractorStrategy: An email address, a phone number or a name chosen as a key — each unique today and mutable tomorrow. The consequence must be stated, not just the choice.

factStatement: A query names the columns it wants back, and every matching row supplies them.
familyName: What columns a query returns
measurementObjective: Given a table and a query, say which columns come back.
distractorStrategy: All columns returned where two were named; the rows filtered when no condition was given; the column order assumed to follow the table rather than the query.
notes: Show the table and the query in the stem throughout this skill.

factStatement: The clauses of a query must appear in a fixed order, whatever order they are thought of in.
familyName: Recognising a correctly ordered query
measurementObjective: Identify which of several queries is written in a valid order.
distractorStrategy: Filtering placed after ordering; grouping placed before filtering; ordering placed before the table is named. The one syntax family admitted, because a wrong order stops the query running at all.
notes: The only deliberate syntax family in the skill.

factStatement: A condition keeps the rows that satisfy it and discards the rest.
familyName: How many rows a condition keeps
measurementObjective: Given a table and a condition, say how many rows come back.
distractorStrategy: A boundary row included or excluded wrongly; the count of columns given; rows with a missing value in the tested column assumed to match. Include a boundary value in the data.

factStatement: Conditions joined by and must both hold; joined by or, either suffices.
familyName: How many rows a combined condition keeps
measurementObjective: Given a table and a combined condition, say which rows come back.
distractorStrategy: and and or swapped; a negation applied to only the first condition; the rows satisfying either given for an and. Data must distinguish all four cases.

factStatement: Rows come back in a defined order only when one is asked for, and ties are not broken by anything unstated.
familyName: The order rows come back in
measurementObjective: Given data and an ordering, give the sequence of rows.
distractorStrategy: Descending read as ascending; ties assumed to keep insertion order; ordering assumed to apply before filtering. Include tied values.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM10.

factStatement: A summary function turns many rows into one value.
familyName: What a summary function returns
measurementObjective: Given a table, give the count, total or average a query returns.
distractorStrategy: Rows with a missing value counted in an average — the D4 case, since it changes the divisor; the count of all rows given where a column was counted; the total given where the average was asked. Data must include a missing value.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM08 and is where that fact earns its place.

factStatement: Grouping produces one summary row per distinct value of the grouping column.
familyName: How many rows a grouped query returns
measurementObjective: Given data and a grouped query, say how many rows come back and what each holds.
distractorStrategy: One row returned in total; one row per original row; the number of groups counted wrongly because a value repeats. The result must be countable from the shown data.

factStatement: Filtering rows before grouping and filtering groups afterwards give different answers.
familyName: Deciding where a filter belongs
measurementObjective: Given a requirement, say whether the condition applies to rows or to groups.
distractorStrategy: A group condition placed on rows; a row condition placed on groups; both assumed interchangeable. A requirement mentioning a count is a group condition and must be recognised as such.

factStatement: A query returns repeated values unless duplicates are explicitly removed.
familyName: Reasoning about repeated values in a result
measurementObjective: Given data, say how many rows come back with and without duplicate removal.
distractorStrategy: Duplicates assumed removed automatically; removal assumed to apply per column rather than per row; the count of distinct values given where all rows were asked for.

factStatement: A row whose tested column is missing satisfies neither a condition nor its negation.
familyName: Reasoning about missing values in a condition
measurementObjective: Given data with missing values, say which rows a condition returns.
distractorStrategy: Missing rows returned by the negated condition — the case that surprises everybody; missing treated as zero; missing treated as matching everything. The row counts must not add up naively, which is the lesson.
notes: The strongest family in the skill for exposing a wrong mental model.

factStatement: Combining tables matches rows on a linking column, and rows without a match are left out unless asked for.
familyName: How many rows a two-table query returns
measurementObjective: Given two small tables, give the number of rows a combined query returns.
distractorStrategy: The sum of the row counts; the product, which is what happens with no matching condition; unmatched rows counted as included. Both tables must contain an unmatched row.
notes: Depends on DB_FAM11.

factStatement: A question stated in words determines what the query must select, filter and group.
familyName: Choosing the query that answers a question
measurementObjective: Given a question in words and several queries, choose the one that answers it exactly.
distractorStrategy: A query answering a nearby question; one correct but returning extra columns; one whose filter is off at the boundary. All must be valid queries, so the reasoning is about meaning.

factStatement: Too many rows, too few, or a wrong total each point to a specific fault in the query.
familyName: Diagnosing a query from its wrong result
measurementObjective: Given a query and a result that is wrong in a stated way, identify the fault.
distractorStrategy: A missing match condition, which multiplies rows; a filter at the wrong stage, which changes a total; a missing value, which changes an average. Each produces a different wrongness and the stem must say which.
notes: A missing match condition producing a row explosion is the canonical D5 stem.

factStatement: A query matching nothing returns an empty result, and a summary over nothing is not zero for every function.
familyName: Reasoning about a query that matches nothing
measurementObjective: Say what a summary query returns when no rows match.
distractorStrategy: An error assumed; every summary assumed to return zero, when a count does and an average does not; no rows assumed to mean no result row at all. The count/average difference is the measurement.

factStatement: Two queries can return the same rows for this data and differ for other data.
familyName: Judging whether two queries always agree
measurementObjective: Decide whether two queries always return the same result, and describe data that separates them.
distractorStrategy: A pair differing only when a value is missing; a pair differing only when a row is unmatched; a genuinely equivalent pair. Reasoning beyond the shown data is the measurement.

factStatement: A network carries data between machines that each have an address.
familyName: Recognising what a network provides
measurementObjective: Identify what is needed for two machines to exchange data.
distractorStrategy: A network described as the internet; as requiring a browser; as needing both machines switched on at the same instant for any exchange. Complements HCW_FAM11 at a technical level.

factStatement: A machine is reached by an address; a name is a convenience that must be turned into one.
familyName: Distinguishing a name from an address
measurementObjective: Say which of a name and an address the network uses to route data.
distractorStrategy: The name assumed to be used directly; the address assumed to be the same thing as the name; one name assumed to mean one machine forever.

factStatement: A port distinguishes different services on the same machine.
familyName: Recognising what a port distinguishes
measurementObjective: Say what a port identifies and what happens when two services want the same one.
distractorStrategy: A port assumed to identify a machine; assumed to be a physical socket; two services assumed able to share one. This is exactly the local-development confusion a first-year hits.

conceptName: Turning a name into an address
factStatement: Before a request can be sent, the name must be looked up to find the address.
familyName: Ordering lookup and request
measurementObjective: Put the steps of reaching a named machine in order.
distractorStrategy: The request assumed sent to the name directly; lookup assumed to happen after connecting; lookup assumed to happen once for all sites.

factStatement: An address that means "this machine" or "this network" cannot be reached from elsewhere.
familyName: Reasoning about who can reach an address
measurementObjective: Say whether a described machine can be reached from another network.
distractorStrategy: A local address assumed shareable — the "it works on my machine" belief; a same-network address assumed reachable from the internet; a public address assumed private.
notes: The first genuinely useful networking fact for someone running a local server.

factStatement: Data is split into pieces that travel separately and are reassembled on arrival.
familyName: Reasoning about data arriving in pieces
measurementObjective: Say what can happen to the pieces in transit and what the receiver must do.
distractorStrategy: Data assumed to travel as one unit; pieces assumed to arrive in order always; a lost piece assumed to lose everything. Out-of-order arrival is the productive case.

factStatement: One kind of transport checks that everything arrived and in order; another does not, and is faster for it.
familyName: Reasoning about guaranteed against fast delivery
measurementObjective: Given a use, say which kind of delivery suits it and what is given up.
distractorStrategy: Guaranteed delivery chosen for live video, where lateness is worse than loss; unguaranteed chosen for a file transfer; the choice justified by speed alone with no mention of loss. No protocol names required.

factStatement: Data crosses several machines on the way, none of which is the destination.
familyName: Reasoning about the path data takes
measurementObjective: Say what the machines along the path do and do not do.
distractorStrategy: A direct connection assumed; intermediaries assumed to read or store the content; the path assumed identical in both directions. The last is a genuine and useful surprise.

factStatement: Addressing, delivery and the meaning of the data are separate responsibilities.
familyName: Assigning a responsibility to a layer
measurementObjective: Given a described job, say which layer of responsibility it belongs to.
distractorStrategy: Retransmission attributed to addressing; the meaning of the content attributed to delivery; encryption attributed to routing. Responsibilities in words, never a numbered model to recite.
notes: Deliberately not a layer-model recall family; builds on HCW_FAM13 on abstraction.

factStatement: Capacity is shared, so one heavy user affects others, and distance adds delay independently of capacity.
familyName: Distinguishing capacity from delay
measurementObjective: Given a symptom, say whether capacity or delay explains it.
distractorStrategy: More capacity offered as the fix for a delay problem — the commonest real confusion; delay blamed for a slow large download; both treated as one quantity called speed.

conceptName: Turning a name into an address
factStatement: A lookup result is remembered for a time, so a changed address is not seen immediately.
familyName: Reasoning about a remembered lookup
measurementObjective: Say what happens after a name is pointed at a new address.
distractorStrategy: The change assumed instant everywhere; assumed never to propagate; the browser cache blamed rather than the lookup. Complements BR_FAM06 at a different layer.

factStatement: Traffic can be blocked by port or by destination, at either end or anywhere between.
familyName: Reasoning about where traffic was blocked
measurementObjective: Given that a connection fails from one place and works from another, say where the block is.
distractorStrategy: The server blamed where the client network blocks; the name lookup blamed where the port is closed; the application blamed. The "works for me" asymmetry is the evidence.

factStatement: A failure to resolve, to connect, or to get a reply are different symptoms pointing to different stages.
familyName: Locating the stage a connection failed at
measurementObjective: Given the symptom, identify which stage failed and what to check.
distractorStrategy: A name failure diagnosed as a server fault; a closed port diagnosed as a name failure; a slow reply diagnosed as a failure. D5 gives a case where the name resolves and nothing answers, which has two plausible causes separated by one detail.
notes: The most practically useful family in the skill.

factStatement: Anything crossing a network unencrypted can be read by whoever handles it on the way.
familyName: Judging who can see what crosses a network
measurementObjective: Given a described situation, decide what a party on the path can learn.
distractorStrategy: Encryption assumed to hide which site was contacted; a private network assumed to make traffic unreadable; a password assumed safe because the page looked private. Extends HP_FAM10 to the network path.

factStatement: Making a local service reachable from elsewhere requires a reachable address and an open path to its port.
familyName: Reasoning about what makes a service reachable
measurementObjective: Given a service that works locally and not remotely, choose what must change.
distractorStrategy: Sharing the local address; changing the port with no path opened; assuming a public name is sufficient without a reachable address. Every option must be something a student would actually try.
notes: Genuine transfer: it requires CN_FAM05, CN_FAM03 and CN_FAM12 together.
